match.reason: No bank point teaches how a change affects different stakeholders: the closest, Stakeholders, covers who stakeholders are and how their wants clash, not the effects of change, and the other cards cover workplace stakeholders or how to manage change.

draft.title: Effects of change on stakeholders
card: A stakeholder is any person or group affected by what a business does. When a business changes, each stakeholder group can be affected in a different way.
Managers and employees
Managers may gain new responsibilities or face more pressure to deliver results. Employees may gain new skills, or face job loss, new tasks or changed hours.
Customers and suppliers
Customers may get lower prices or better products, or find the service has got worse. Suppliers may win bigger orders, or lose a contract if the business changes what it buys.
Community
The community can gain local jobs or lose them if a site closes. One change can help one group and harm another at the same time.
draft.remember: One change can help some stakeholders and harm others, so managers should weigh each group's effects.

a.q: Which statement best describes how a change affects stakeholders?
opts: The effects can differ from group to group
Every stakeholder group is affected the same way
Only employees are affected by a change
A change that helps one group helps all groups
a.why: Each stakeholder group has different interests, so one change can help some groups and harm others. The option saying every group is affected the same way is wrong because a change that helps customers can still cost employees their jobs.
a.clue: Think about who gains and who loses from one change.

b.q: Mia's bakery chain in Geelong closes two small shops and opens one large automated bakery. Which effect is a likely benefit to one stakeholder group but a cost to another?
opts: Cheaper bread for customers, but fewer jobs for staff
Lower prices for customers and more choice for customers
Fewer jobs for staff and fewer jobs for the community
New skills for staff and new skills for managers
b.why: Cheaper bread helps customers, while closing the shops may cost staff their jobs. That is a gain for one group and a loss for another. The other options list effects that fall on the same side, so none of them shows a benefit for one group and a cost for another.
b.clue: Look for one option where the two groups are affected in opposite ways.

a.best: The effects can differ from group to group

b.best: Cheaper bread for customers, but fewer jobs for staff

problems.detail: The right option is the only one with a qualifier ('can'). Every distractor is an absolute ('Only', 'all', 'Every'), so a student can pick it without knowing the idea. The clue about 'who gains and who loses' also points straight at it, which makes the question very easy for Year 12.

The right option is the only one built on a contrast ('..., but ...'). The other three all use 'and', so the right answer stands out from its structure alone, and the clue ('opposite ways') reinforces this.

check.summary: The content is accurate. In both questions, though, the right option stands out from its form: in (a) it is the only hedged statement among absolutes, and in (b) it is the only one with 'but'. Students could answer both without knowing the idea.

a.q: A café chain in Ballarat stops buying milk from a local dairy and switches to a cheaper national company. How is the local dairy best described?
opts: A supplier, which loses the chain's orders
A supplier, which wins bigger orders
A customer, which pays higher prices
The community, which gains local jobs
a.why: The dairy sold milk to the café chain, so it is a supplier, and the change means it loses that contract. The supplier that wins bigger orders is the national company, not the local dairy.
a.clue: What did the dairy do for the café chain before the change?

b.q: Mia's bakery chain in Geelong closes two small shops and opens one large automated bakery. Which pairing of a likely benefit and a likely cost fits this change?
opts: Customers get cheaper bread, some shop staff lose jobs
Shop staff gain more jobs, customers pay more for bread
Customers get cheaper bread, managers have fewer duties
Shop staff gain more hours, customers get worse bread
b.why: Automation can cut costs, so customers may pay less, while closing shops can cost staff their jobs. The option about managers is tempting because cheaper bread is right, but running a large new site is more likely to give managers new responsibilities, not fewer.
b.clue: Think about what automation and closing shops do to costs and jobs.

a.best: A supplier, which loses the chain's orders

b.best: Customers get cheaper bread, some shop staff lose jobs
